lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- Language Under Pressure
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 14 -- Language Under Pressure
phases: Two Ways to Lose a Number

listenings.text: There are two ways to lose credibility with a number, and only one of them ever gets pointed out to you. The first is overstating. You give a figure you cannot deliver, somebody holds you to it, and everyone remembers. That one is loud, it is embarrassing, and it is survivable, because you can see it happening. The second is quieter and far more expensive. You hedge everything. Every figure comes with three conditions, nothing is ever final, and after a year people stop asking you for numbers at all. Nobody will ever tell you this is happening. They will simply route the question to somebody who answers it. What good executives do is neither. They are precise about the degree. This I will stand behind. This is our working assumption. This is indicative and I would not quote it. Three sentences, three different levels of certainty, and every one of them defensible.

The thing nobody warns you about is that a hedge does not travel. In my own language I had thirty years of practice at sounding exactly as certain as I was. In English I had two settings: sure, and sorry. So I would either give a flat number, which was more than I meant, or I would apologise my way around it, which was less. Both were misread. The flat number became a commitment. The apology became doubt about the underlying business, when the only doubt I had was about the decimal. What fixed it was small. I stopped improvising the certainty and started choosing the phrase before the call. It appears that. On the evidence we have. This is provisional. Four or five phrases, used deliberately, and suddenly the room could hear the difference between a number I was guessing at and a number I would defend.

extra_audio.text: The retention figure is eighty-four percent, and that is a number I will stand behind. On the industrial book, our working assumption is six percent. On the evidence we have, capacity would appear to be tightening. A harder market in twenty twenty-seven is plausible, and it is not yet a forecast.

reading.rtitle: Q4 Market Assessment -- Large Risks, Brazil
paras: This assessment covers the fourth quarter and the first view of 2027. It is written to a single rule: every figure in it is labelled with how much we know. Where a number is final, it is stated plainly. Where it is not, it is called provisional or indicative, and the reader is told what would have to happen for it to move.

Two things can be said with confidence. Renewal retention in large risks closed the quarter at eighty-four percent, and that figure will not move. Rate on the industrial portfolio rose five point one percent year on year, and this directorate would defend that number in front of the market. Neither of the two is an estimate; both have been reconciled twice.

The 2027 outlook is a different kind of statement. On the evidence we have, capacity in the region would appear to be tightening, and a harder market next year is plausible. It is not yet a forecast, and it should not be read as one. The pricing assumptions in the appendix are indicative: they show the shape of the movement rather than the figure, and the figure itself stays provisional until the December run-off closes. Directionally we are where this directorate said we would be in July; the exact number we do not yet have.

Our working assumption for planning is a six percent rate increase across the industrial book. It is an assumption and not a commitment, and two things would move it: a reinsurance renewal above the level currently indicated, and any further deterioration in the southern accounts. The order of magnitude is reliable; the decimal is not. If the group needs a figure it can hold this directorate to before December, we will give one, and it will be lower than six percent, deliberately. A number you are held to has to survive a bad month, not only a good one.
reading.source: Commercial Directorate, Brazil -- to Group, Milan
